exercises.title: A report that's returning way more rows than the dimension table it's summarizing
exercises.situation: In a code review, a teammate points out that a report query built on top of a customer dimension table is returning several times more rows than that dimension table actually has. Explain what's happening and how you'd describe the fix.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I think the join is pulling in extra rows somehow. I'll just throw a DISTINCT on the query so it stops showing duplicates.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This treats a predictable consequence of SQL's set logic as a mystery bug and reaches for DISTINCT as a bandage instead of naming what's actually happening: a one-to-many join multiplying each dimension row once per matching row on the other side. It never names the join type in use, never considers pre-aggregating the many-side table before joining, and DISTINCT can silently mask a genuine duplicate-data problem at the same time it hides the expected fan-out — which is worse than not fixing it at all, because now it looks fixed.
exercises.professionalResponse: Before changing anything, I'd confirm the relationship between the two tables: if the dimension table is joined directly to a fact or transaction table on a one-to-many key, every dimension row appears once for every matching row on the many side — that's not a bug, it's exactly what an INNER JOIN or LEFT JOIN is supposed to do with that cardinality, commonly called fan-out. I'd verify this with a quick COUNT(*) on the dimension table alone versus the joined result, and a COUNT per key, to confirm the multiplication lines up with the many-side row counts rather than something stranger, like an accidental cross join or a predicate matching the wrong column — a true Cartesian product. Once confirmed, the real fix depends on what the report needs: if it needs one row per dimension member, I'd pre-aggregate the many-side table in a CTE before joining, so the join itself can't multiply rows. I'd specifically avoid DISTINCT as the fix, because it only hides the symptom — if there's a genuine duplicate-row problem in the source data on top of the expected fan-out, DISTINCT would mask that too, and the report would quietly show wrong numbers that look clean. I'd also check whether an INNER JOIN is dropping dimension members with zero matching activity when the report actually wants to show them as zero, which is a separate decision from the fan-out question and would call for a LEFT JOIN instead. I'd validate the fix by re-running the row-count comparison and spot-checking one known dimension member's numbers by hand against the aggregated result.

vocabulary.definition: A join that returns only rows where the join condition finds a match in both tables.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It silently drops dimension members that have no matching rows on the other side, which is often the real reason a report looks like it's missing data.
vocabulary.example: I'd check whether this is an INNER JOIN, since dimension members with zero activity would simply not appear.

vocabulary.definition: A join that keeps every row from the left table and fills in NULLs for any columns from the right table where no match exists.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's the right choice when a report needs to show every dimension member, including ones with no matching activity.
vocabulary.example: If the report needs to show customers with zero orders as zero rather than disappearing, this should be a LEFT JOIN.

vocabulary.definition: The deliberate decision of which join type fits what the result set is actually supposed to represent, rather than defaulting to whichever one happens to return rows.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: Picking a join type by habit instead of by what the report needs is exactly how fan-out and silently-dropped rows both happen.
vocabulary.example: I'd choose INNER vs. LEFT JOIN based on whether zero-activity members should disappear or show as zero, not by default.

vocabulary.definition: The full, unconstrained set of row combinations produced when a join has no effective matching condition — every row on one side paired with every row on the other.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's the more extreme version of unexpected row multiplication, usually caused by a missing or wrong join predicate rather than a genuine one-to-many relationship.
vocabulary.example: I'd rule out a true Cartesian product — a missing or incorrect join condition — before assuming this is ordinary fan-out.

vocabulary.definition: The specific, well-behaved case where a correct one-to-many join duplicates each row on the one-side once per matching row on the many-side — not an error, just set logic.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: Recognizing fan-out as expected behavior, not a bug, is what keeps you from chasing a nonexistent defect in the join logic itself. This course names the more extreme Cartesian-product case directly; fan-out from a legitimate one-to-many relationship is the milder, far more common cousin it doesn't give a separate name to.

vocabulary.definition: Summarizing the many-side table down to one row per key — in a CTE or subquery — before joining it to the one-side table, so the join itself cannot multiply rows.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's the structural fix for fan-out, as opposed to DISTINCT, which only hides the multiplied rows after the fact without changing why they were multiplied.

exercises.title: Why 'Snowflake is slow today' isn't a diagnosis
exercises.situation: A stakeholder says the dashboard was slow this morning and concludes 'Snowflake must be having issues.' Explain, precisely, what's actually going on inside Snowflake and how you'd investigate instead of accepting that explanation.
exercises.beginnerResponse: Snowflake's probably just overloaded right now. It should clear up on its own.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: 'Overloaded' isn't a real category of problem in Snowflake's architecture — storage, compute, and the cloud services layer are deliberately separated so one workload's load doesn't degrade another's, and there's no single shared 'Snowflake' resource to be generically overloaded. This answer names no warehouse, no query, and no evidence, and it proposes waiting instead of investigating, which guarantees tomorrow's version of this complaint gets the same non-answer.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd start by identifying which virtual warehouse actually ran the dashboard's queries, since compute in Snowflake is isolated per warehouse rather than shared across the account — if a different warehouse was busy, it has no effect on this one. I'd check whether that warehouse had auto-suspended from inactivity and had to auto-resume for this query, since a cold start adds real, one-time latency before the first query even begins executing. Assuming it was already running, I'd pull up Query Profile and Query History for the specific slow query to see where time was actually spent — scanning more micro-partitions than expected because of poor pruning, waiting in a queue behind other concurrent queries on an undersized warehouse, or simply a large result set. If it's a pruning problem, I'd look at whether the query's filter predicates align with how the table is naturally ordered or clustered. If it's queueing, the real fix is warehouse sizing or concurrency, not 'Snowflake having a bad day.' I'd report back with the specific cause and a specific fix, not a wait-and-see.

exercises.title: Why one dbt model takes forty minutes while the rest take seconds
exercises.situation: A teammate asks why one model in the nightly dbt job takes forty minutes to build while most of the project's other models finish in seconds. Explain what's actually going on and what you'd check.
exercises.beginnerResponse: That model's just big, I guess. Maybe we should run it less often so it doesn't slow things down every night.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This accepts the slowness as an unchangeable fact of the data's size rather than checking the model's actual materialization strategy. It never considers that the model might simply be rebuilding its entire history from scratch on every run when it doesn't need to, and 'run it less often' trades away freshness instead of fixing the real cost driver.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd start by checking how this model is actually materialized — its config block will say view, table, incremental, or ephemeral. If it's configured as a table, dbt drops and rebuilds the entire result set from scratch on every single run, which gets more expensive as the underlying data grows, regardless of how little actually changed since yesterday. I'd check whether this model has a reliable high-watermark column, like an updated_at or loaded_at timestamp, that would make it a good candidate for incremental materialization instead — processing only new or changed rows on each run rather than the full history. If it qualifies, I'd convert it and pick an incremental strategy that fits the warehouse and the data's update pattern — merge, delete+insert, or append — and I'd explicitly test it with both an incremental run and a --full-refresh to confirm both paths produce the same result. If the model doesn't have a clean high-watermark and genuinely can't go incremental, I'd also look at whether its real cost is a deeply nested, multi-join query that belongs broken out into an intermediate model instead, since that's a layering problem a materialization change alone won't fix.

vocabulary.definition: A materialization that processes only new or changed rows on each run, instead of rebuilding the model's entire result set from scratch.

vocabulary.definition: The specific method dbt uses to apply incremental changes to the existing table — merge, delete+insert, or append — chosen based on the warehouse and the data's update pattern.

vocabulary.definition: A dbt run with the --full-refresh flag, which forces an incremental model to rebuild from scratch exactly once, bypassing its usual incremental filter.

vocabulary.definition: The practice of splitting dbt projects into staging (light cleanup), intermediate (reusable business logic), and marts (final, consumption-ready) layers.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: A model that's slow because it's doing too much work in one place is often a layering problem, not a materialization problem.

exercises.situation: A new hire describes an Azure Data Factory setup to you as, 'We just set up the connection to pull the data and run the job.' Explain, precisely, what's actually involved using the correct terms.

First, a linked service defines the connection itself — the credentials and endpoint for, say, an Azure SQL Database or Blob Storage account — and it's reusable across any number of datasets and pipelines that need that same source. Second, a dataset is a named pointer to a specific piece of data at that linked service — a particular table, container, or file path, along with its schema — so the same linked service can back many different datasets. Third, the pipeline is the actual orchestrated unit of work: a sequence of activities, most commonly a Copy Activity, that reads from a source dataset and writes to a sink dataset, plus whatever control-flow logic — conditions, loops, error handling — the movement needs. On top of that, a trigger decides when the pipeline actually runs — on a schedule, in response to an event, or manually — which is a separate concept from the pipeline itself. Keeping these separate matters practically: if the credentials change, I only touch the linked service; if the destination changes, I touch the dataset or the pipeline's sink, not the connection.

exercises.title: Calling an orchestrated pipeline 'the script that runs every night'
exercises.situation: A colleague describes an Airflow-based pipeline as, 'It's just the script that runs every night to load the data.' Explain, precisely, what Airflow is actually doing, using the correct vocabulary.
exercises.beginnerResponse: Yeah, it's basically a script that runs on a schedule every night and loads the data into the warehouse.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This describes Airflow as if it were a single linear script, when the entire point of Airflow is that it's orchestrating a graph of independent, dependent tasks — not running one undifferentiated block of code. It never distinguishes a DAG's definition from one of its actual runs, never names what an operator is, and gives no sense of how failure in one task affects the others, which matters enormously the first time something in the middle breaks.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd describe it as a DAG — a directed acyclic graph — which is a definition of a set of tasks and the dependencies between them, not a single script executing top to bottom. Each task in that DAG is created by instantiating an operator, which is a template for a specific kind of work — a PythonOperator for a Python function, a BashOperator for a shell command, and so on — so 'the script' is really several distinct tasks, each with its own operator, connected by explicit dependency edges that say which tasks must finish before others can start. The DAG itself is just the definition; every time the scheduler actually executes it — nightly, on this schedule — that's a separate DAG run, made up of individual task instances, each with its own status: success, failed, retrying, or upstream_failed. If one task in the middle fails, Airflow doesn't treat the whole thing as one failed script — only that task and whatever depends on it are affected, and trigger rules control exactly how failures propagate, which is very different from a single script that just dies partway through. Tasks can also pass small pieces of data between each other using XComs, which is how later tasks know what earlier ones produced without a shared global variable. The real value of describing it this way is that it tells you exactly where to look when something breaks — which task, which DAG run, not 'the script.'

exercises.title: Warehouse credits spiked overnight and nobody knows why
exercises.situation: Finance flags that Snowflake compute costs tripled last night compared to a normal night, and asks you to find out what happened. Explain how you'd investigate.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd probably just make the warehouse smaller so it uses fewer credits going forward.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This jumps to a fix — shrinking the warehouse — before identifying what actually consumed the credits, and it could easily make things worse: if the real cause was one genuinely heavy, necessary workload, a smaller warehouse would just make that workload slower without saving anything, or force it to queue. There's no mention of looking at what actually ran, no distinction between a one-off event and a new ongoing pattern, and no way to confirm the fix addresses the real cause.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd start in Query History, filtered to the warehouse and the time window in question, sorted by credits consumed or execution time, to see exactly what ran. I'm looking for one of a few patterns: a single very expensive query or a small number of them, a much higher volume of normal-sized queries than usual, or a warehouse that spent an unusual amount of time running at all because it kept getting resumed instead of staying idle-then-suspended. If it's one expensive query, I'd open its Query Profile to see whether it's scanning far more data than expected — possibly from a change upstream, like a lost filter or a table that grew much larger than before. If it's volume, I'd check whether a new job, a retried failed job, or a change in a scheduled task's frequency is now running more often than intended. I'd also check the resource monitor configuration, since a monitor set to notify rather than suspend wouldn't have stopped the spend even if it was configured correctly. Once I've identified the actual driver, I'd decide on the fix that matches it specifically — fixing a missing filter, correcting a mis-scheduled task, or, only if the workload is genuinely larger and legitimately needs it, resizing the warehouse — rather than shrinking the warehouse by default, which treats every possible cause the same way.

exercises.title: An incremental dbt model is quietly producing duplicate rows
exercises.situation: Someone notices that a mart model's row count is higher than it should be, and traces it to an incremental dbt model upstream that appears to be inserting the same records more than once. Explain how you'd investigate and fix it.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd just run a --full-refresh on it. That rebuilds the whole thing so the duplicates should go away.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: A full refresh clears out the existing duplicates, but it does nothing to explain why they appeared in the first place, and if the underlying cause is still there, the model will quietly start producing duplicates again on the very next incremental run. This treats the symptom as the problem and skips any investigation of the model's incremental strategy, its filter logic, or whether its unique key assumption is actually true.
exercises.professionalResponse: Before rebuilding anything, I'd look at how this model is actually filtering for 'new or changed' rows in its incremental logic — usually a condition like a comparison against the max loaded timestamp already in the target table. A common cause of duplicates is that filter being too loose, re-selecting rows from the source that were already loaded in a previous run, combined with an incremental strategy of append, which just adds rows rather than updating or replacing matching ones. I'd check the model's configured incremental strategy — append, delete+insert, or merge — since append has no concept of 'this row already exists,' while merge or delete+insert are built to handle that correctly if given the right unique key. If it's configured as merge, I'd check whether the declared unique key is actually unique in the source data; if the source has legitimate duplicate values on what the model assumes is a unique key, merge will still produce duplicates because its assumption is wrong, not because the strategy itself is broken. Once I've identified whether it's the filter, the strategy choice, or a broken unique-key assumption, I'd fix that specific cause, then do the full refresh once to clear the existing duplicates — in that order, not as the fix on its own. I'd validate by running the model incrementally again on fresh data and confirming the output's row count matches what a manual, independent count of the source would predict.

exercises.title: A Data Factory pipeline fails a couple of nights a week, for no obvious reason
exercises.situation: A nightly Data Factory pipeline has started failing intermittently — maybe twice a week, with no obvious pattern — while succeeding the rest of the time. Explain how you'd investigate.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd just add a retry to the pipeline so it tries again automatically if it fails. That should take care of it.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: Adding a retry without knowing why it's failing treats every possible cause identically, including ones a retry can't fix — like a genuine schema change or a permissions problem, which will just fail the same way every single retry. This never opens the Monitor hub to see which activity actually failed and why, and there's no distinction drawn between a transient issue a retry would plausibly fix and a persistent one it won't.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd start in the Monitor hub, looking specifically at the failed runs to see which activity failed and what error message it recorded — that's the single most informative piece of evidence, and skipping it means guessing. If the error points to a transient network or connectivity issue — a timeout reaching a source system, for instance — that's genuinely a good candidate for a retry policy with backoff, since the same operation often succeeds a few seconds later. But if the error is something like a schema mismatch, an authentication failure, or a resource that temporarily didn't exist, a retry will just fail the same way every time and waste time before the pipeline eventually reports failure anyway. I'd check whether the failures cluster around a specific activity — Copy Activity failures often point to the source or sink being briefly unavailable, while a Data Flow failure might point to a memory or compute sizing issue under certain data volumes. I'd also check whether this is tied to a self-hosted integration runtime if one is in play, since those can fail due to the on-premises host's own resource constraints in ways a cloud-only pipeline wouldn't. Once the actual cause is identified, I'd apply a retry policy only where it's actually appropriate, and separately fix whatever is genuinely broken — and I'd set up an alert on this pipeline's failures so we know within minutes next time, rather than finding out when someone notices stale data.

exercises.title: An Airflow DAG is stuck, and nobody's sure if it's actually running
exercises.situation: A nightly Airflow DAG that normally finishes in twenty minutes has been showing as 'running' for three hours, and the on-call engineer isn't sure whether it's actually stuck or just slow. Explain how you'd investigate.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd just manually mark it as failed and trigger it again. That usually gets things moving.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This skips finding out which task is actually the problem, so the DAG could get re-triggered and hang at exactly the same place for exactly the same unaddressed reason. It also risks real consequences if the DAG isn't actually stuck — forcing a failure and re-run on a job that's genuinely still working could duplicate work downstream if the tasks aren't idempotent, which this answer never even considers.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd start in the Airflow UI's graph or grid view for this specific DAG run to see exactly which task is in a running, queued, or up_for_retry state, rather than treating the whole DAG as one undifferentiated 'stuck' thing. If one task has been running far longer than its historical average, I'd open that task's logs directly to see what it's actually doing — waiting on a sensor that hasn't met its condition yet, stuck in a long-running query against the source system, or genuinely hung with no new log output at all. A sensor waiting past its expected window is a very different problem from a task that's hung: the first might mean the upstream data simply isn't ready yet and the DAG is behaving correctly, while the second means something needs to be killed and investigated. I'd also check whether this looks like a resource contention issue — multiple DAGs or tasks competing for the same connection pool or worker slots — versus a problem specific to this one task's logic. Before manually marking anything as failed and re-triggering, I'd confirm whether the tasks involved are idempotent, since forcing a failure and rerun on a task that's genuinely still in-flight and not idempotent could duplicate the work it's already partway through. Once I've identified the specific cause, I'd apply the right fix — clearing just that task instance if it's genuinely hung, adjusting a sensor's timeout or trigger rule if it's a legitimate wait, or addressing the resource contention directly — and I'd watch the next run closely to confirm it completes in its normal window.

exercises.title: A Power BI dataset's scheduled refresh just started failing
exercises.situation: A Power BI semantic model's scheduled refresh, which has worked reliably for months, started failing every night this week. Explain how you'd investigate.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd just try refreshing it manually from the Service and see if that works.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This treats 'try it again' as an investigation, when a manual refresh succeeding or failing doesn't by itself explain anything — it never looks at the actual error message, never considers what changed this week specifically, and gives no plan for what to do differently if the manual refresh fails the same way.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd start by reading the actual refresh failure error from the refresh history in the Power BI Service, since the error message itself usually points directly at the category of problem — a credential or authentication failure, a gateway connectivity issue, or a data-source error like a changed column or missing table. I'd ask what changed this week specifically: a password rotation on the source system, a gateway update or restart, a schema change upstream, or a new row-level security role added to the model, since failures that start suddenly after months of success are almost always tied to a specific change, not random instability. If the model depends on an on-premises data gateway, I'd check the gateway's own status and logs, since gateway downtime or a version mismatch produces a refresh failure that has nothing to do with the dataset's own queries. If it's a credential issue, I'd check whether the data source credentials stored in the Service need to be re-entered — those can silently expire or be invalidated by a password change on the source side without any obvious warning in the dataset itself. I'd also consider whether the refresh is simply taking longer than the service's timeout now, if upstream data volume has grown, which is a performance problem wearing a failure message. Once I've identified the actual category, I'd fix that specific thing, then confirm by watching the next one or two scheduled refreshes complete successfully rather than relying on a single manual retry.

exercises.title: Deciding how big to make a Snowflake warehouse — and whether 'bigger' is even the right axis
exercises.situation: A team lead asks you to recommend a virtual warehouse setup for a new reporting workload that will be queried by dozens of analysts throughout the business day. Explain how you'd approach that decision.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd just pick a big warehouse size so it's definitely fast enough for everyone.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This treats warehouse size as the only lever available and assumes bigger always means better, when warehouse size and warehouse concurrency are actually two different problems with two different solutions. It ignores cost entirely, ignores whether the workload is dominated by query complexity or by simultaneous user volume, and gives no plan for validating the choice once real usage starts.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd start by separating two different questions that 'big enough' conflates: how much compute does any single query need to run quickly, and how many queries need to run at the same time without queueing behind each other. Warehouse size — Small, Medium, Large, and so on — addresses the first question, since a bigger warehouse has more compute to throw at a single complex query. But dozens of analysts querying throughout the day is primarily a concurrency problem, not a single-query-complexity problem, and oversizing one warehouse for that doesn't actually solve concurrency — if enough queries land at the same moment, they'll still queue behind each other regardless of how large the warehouse is, while the business pays for a bigger warehouse sitting idle the rest of the time. I'd recommend starting with a moderately sized warehouse matched to the actual complexity of a typical report query, validated with realistic test queries and Query Profile, and I'd factor in auto-suspend to avoid paying for idle time between analysts' queries throughout the day. If concurrency genuinely becomes the bottleneck once real usage data comes in — visible as queueing in Query History during peak hours — the right lever is Snowflake's multi-cluster warehouse feature, which adds additional clusters of the same size to absorb concurrent load, rather than resizing the single warehouse bigger. I'd present this as a starting configuration to be validated against real usage patterns in the first few weeks, not a one-time guess, and I'd set up a specific check of peak-hour queueing as the signal for whether to add clusters.

exercises.title: Explaining why a dbt project has three model layers instead of one
exercises.situation: A stakeholder looking at a dbt project's file structure asks why there are staging, intermediate, and marts folders instead of just writing one query per report. Explain the architectural reasoning.
exercises.beginnerResponse: It's just how dbt projects are usually organized. We follow that pattern too.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This defers to convention without explaining what problem the convention actually solves, which means it can't defend the structure if someone pushes back with 'but one query per report would be simpler.' It gives no account of what each layer is actually responsible for, and no sense of what would go wrong without the separation.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd explain the three layers by what each one is responsible for, not just that it's conventional. Staging models do the minimal, mechanical cleanup closest to the raw source — renaming columns, fixing types, light filtering — and nothing business-specific; there's exactly one staging model per source table, so any future change to the raw source only needs to be absorbed in one place. Intermediate models build reusable business logic on top of staging — joining a few related staging models together, computing a shared calculation — logic that more than one downstream report might need. Marts are the final, report-ready layer, built on staging and intermediate models, shaped specifically for how a particular report or dashboard needs to consume the data. The alternative — one big query per report — means that if ten reports all need 'active customer' defined the same way, that definition gets copy-pasted into ten separate queries, and when the business definition of 'active' changes, someone has to find and update it in ten places, with a high chance of missing one and producing reports that quietly disagree with each other. With the layered approach, that logic lives once in an intermediate model, and every mart and report built from it inherits the fix the moment it's updated. The tradeoff is more files and more indirection to navigate, which is a real cost for a very small project, but it's what actually prevents the inconsistency problem at any meaningful scale.

exercises.title: Choosing between Azure Data Factory, SSIS, and Fabric Data Factory for a new pipeline
exercises.situation: A team is starting a new data movement project and asks whether it should be built in Azure Data Factory, classic SSIS, or Fabric Data Factory. Explain how you'd approach that decision.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd just use whichever one we're already most familiar with so we can move faster.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: Familiarity is a real factor, but treating it as the only one skips every actual architectural consideration — where the data and destinations already live, whether the organization is already committed to Fabric, what the on-premises connectivity requirements are, and what each tool is actually suited for. It gives no framework a stakeholder could use to sanity-check the choice, and it would reach the same conclusion regardless of what the project actually needs.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd frame the decision around where the data already lives and where the organization's platform strategy is headed, not just team familiarity. SSIS is a strong fit when the work is squarely on-premises, SQL Server-centric, and there's existing SSIS infrastructure and expertise already in place — it's not cloud-native, so pulling it into a cloud-first strategy usually doesn't make sense for a brand-new project. Azure Data Factory is the right default for cloud-based orchestration and movement across a wide range of Azure and external sources, especially if the organization isn't yet committed to Fabric specifically — it has the most mature connector ecosystem and the most production history of the three. Fabric Data Factory makes sense if the organization has already adopted or is actively moving to Microsoft Fabric, since it shares OneLake as a destination and integrates directly with the rest of the Fabric workspace, which avoids building a bridge between two separate platforms. I'd also factor in connectivity requirements specifically — if there's a genuine on-premises source involved, that affects whether a self-hosted integration runtime is needed, which both ADF and Fabric support but changes the deployment story either way. Given that this is a new project without existing SSIS infrastructure constraints, I'd lean toward ADF or Fabric Data Factory based specifically on where the organization's broader platform direction is heading, and I'd present that reasoning rather than defaulting to the team's current comfort zone.

exercises.title: Explaining why an orchestration tool sits on top of Snowflake Tasks and ADF triggers, instead of replacing them
exercises.skillTag: Orchestration Architecture Across the Modern Data Stack
exercises.situation: A stakeholder asks why the team is introducing Airflow when Snowflake already has Tasks and Data Factory already has triggers — isn't that redundant? Explain the architectural reasoning.
exercises.beginnerResponse: Airflow's just more powerful, so it's better to use it for everything going forward.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This doesn't explain what Snowflake Tasks or ADF triggers actually do well on their own, doesn't identify the specific gap Airflow is filling, and 'more powerful' isn't a reason by itself — it implies replacing tools that are working fine in their own scope, which is a bigger and riskier change than what's actually needed.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd frame this as adding a coordination layer above several independent systems, not replacing any of them. Snowflake Tasks are genuinely the right tool for scheduling a transformation that lives entirely inside Snowflake — a stream-and-task incremental pipeline doesn't need an external orchestrator watching over it. ADF triggers are similarly well-suited to kicking off a pipeline that's entirely contained within Data Factory. The gap appears specifically when a single logical workflow spans more than one of these systems — for example, a dbt run that needs to happen only after a Snowflake COPY INTO load finishes, which itself depends on an upstream file landing from an ADF pipeline. None of Snowflake Tasks, ADF triggers, or dbt's own scheduling can see across that whole chain or make one system wait correctly on another's real completion status; each can only coordinate within its own walls. Airflow's job is specifically to sit above all of them, calling into Snowflake, dbt, and ADF as needed, tracking the dependencies between those cross-system steps, retrying and alerting at the workflow level, and giving one place to see the entire pipeline's status instead of three separate systems that each only know about their own piece. I'd present this as additive — each tool keeps doing its own job well — rather than a wholesale replacement, since forcing every single-system schedule into Airflow for no reason would just add unnecessary operational overhead for things that were already working.

exercises.title: Choosing between Terraform and Bicep to provision the data platform's Azure infrastructure
exercises.situation: The team needs to provision Azure resources — storage accounts, a Fabric capacity, an Event Hub — as code rather than clicking through the portal, and asks whether to use Terraform or Bicep. Explain how you'd approach that decision.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd just use whichever one is easier to learn so we can get started faster.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: Ease of learning is a real but secondary factor; this skips the actual architectural considerations — whether the environment is Azure-only or multi-cloud, how state is managed, and what the organization's existing tooling investment looks like. It would reach the same shallow conclusion regardless of what the infrastructure or the organization's broader cloud strategy actually needs.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd frame the decision around two main things: whether this is an Azure-only environment or part of a genuinely multi-cloud strategy, and how state management fits into the existing workflow. Bicep is Azure-native, has no concept of other cloud providers, and benefits from a simpler deployment model since Azure itself tracks deployment history — there's less separate state-management machinery to operate. Terraform is cloud-agnostic, using the same core workflow and language across Azure, AWS, GCP, and more, which matters directly if the organization already manages other clouds with Terraform or might need to later; the tradeoff is that Terraform requires actively managing its own state file, typically in remote backend storage, which is an extra piece of infrastructure to get right from day one. For a pipeline that includes a storage account, a Fabric capacity, and an Event Hub — all Azure-native resources with no indication of a multi-cloud requirement — Bicep is a reasonable default specifically because it avoids the state-management overhead for no real multi-cloud benefit. If the organization already has Terraform conventions, modules, and CI/CD patterns in place for provisioning elsewhere, though, consistency with that existing investment can outweigh Bicep's simplicity — introducing a second IaC tool just for this one data platform adds its own cost in the form of two sets of patterns for the team to maintain. I'd present both the Azure-only default and the existing-investment exception, rather than a single flat answer that ignores organizational context.

exercises.title: An executive wants 'a dashboard with everything on it'
exercises.situation: An executive sponsor asks for 'a dashboard that shows everything about our sales performance.' Explain how you'd turn that into an actual, buildable set of requirements.
exercises.beginnerResponse: Sure, I'll just build a dashboard with all the sales data and charts for everything we have.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: Agreeing to 'everything' without clarifying produces a dashboard with no clear purpose, no prioritized KPIs, and a high chance of being rebuilt once the executive sees it and realizes it doesn't actually answer the specific questions they have — because nobody asked what those questions were. There's no mention of audience, decision context, or how success will even be judged.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd treat 'everything' as the start of the conversation, not the requirement itself, and ask what specific decisions this dashboard is meant to support — are they trying to spot underperforming regions, track progress against a quarterly target, understand which products are driving growth, or something else entirely? I'd ask who else will be looking at it and at what cadence, since a dashboard an executive glances at weekly needs a different shape than one an analyst drills into daily. From there, I'd work toward a short, deliberately prioritized set of KPIs rather than every metric available, since a dashboard trying to show everything usually ends up highlighting nothing — the whole point of choosing KPIs is picking the few numbers that actually drive a decision, not cataloguing all of them. I'd propose a layout built around that prioritized set first, with drill-through available for the executive to go deeper on any one number if they want more detail, rather than surfacing every possible breakdown on the main view. I'd also confirm upfront what 'done' looks like — a short review session before the first full build, so I'm not building against my own guess about what 'everything' meant.

exercises.professionalResponse: I'd lead with what matters most to them: the numbers on the dashboard right now are yesterday's, not wrong or corrupted, and I'd give a specific, honest estimate of when fresh data will be available. I'd explain why this happened in terms they can act on: a data quality test caught an unexpected change in the source data — for example, a column that's unexpectedly started allowing null values — and the pipeline deliberately stopped rather than publishing numbers built on data that might not mean what it used to. I'd frame that explicitly as the system working as intended, not failing: it's specifically designed to hold back questionable data rather than publish it silently, which is the opposite of the alternative, worse outcome where nobody notices a data problem until someone makes a decision based on wrong numbers. I'd tell them exactly what's being done — tracing the test failure to its source, confirming whether it's a genuine data issue or an expected change that the test itself needs to be updated for, and specify roughly how long that takes before they see refreshed numbers. If the delay affects a specific deadline they have, I'd ask directly whether that's the case, so I can prioritize accordingly rather than assuming it is or isn't urgent on their behalf.

exercises.title: Explaining to business stakeholders why the new pipeline does ELT instead of ETL
exercises.situation: A business stakeholder who remembers the old on-premises data warehouse process asks why the new pipeline seems to load raw data first and clean it up afterward, instead of cleaning it before loading like the old system did. Explain the tradeoff in terms they'd find useful.
exercises.beginnerResponse: It's just the modern way of doing things now, ELT instead of ETL. The new tools work better that way.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This asserts that the new approach is better without explaining what actually changed or why it matters to the stakeholder specifically — it doesn't mention cost, speed, or flexibility, which are the things a business stakeholder actually cares about, and 'the modern way' isn't a reason, it's a trend claim.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd explain it around what actually changed between the two eras: the old on-premises warehouse had limited, expensive compute, so it made sense to clean and shape data carefully before loading it, since loading bad or oversized data was costly to redo. A cloud data warehouse like Snowflake separates storage from compute and can scale compute up or down on demand, which flips that economics — loading raw data first is now cheap and fast, and the heavier transformation work happens afterward, inside the warehouse, where it can use that elastic compute instead of a separate, limited transformation server. The practical benefit for the business is that raw data lands quickly and is available for inspection immediately, which matters when something needs investigating — with the old approach, if a transformation step dropped or altered something incorrectly before loading, the original raw version might not even exist anywhere to check against. It also means we can change how data is transformed without having to re-extract it from the source system each time, since the raw copy is already sitting in the warehouse. The tradeoff worth being upfront about is that raw data is available before it's been validated or cleaned, so there's a window where what's sitting in the raw layer shouldn't be treated as business-ready — which is exactly why there's a separate, clearly labeled layer for cleaned, validated data that reports should actually be built on.

I'd give a specific, honest estimate for when the fix will be ready and the next deploy attempt will run, rather than an open-ended 'as soon as we can.' exercises.title: Proving a Snowflake query tuning fix actually worked, not just that it feels faster
exercises.situation: After changing a table's clustering key to address a slow report query, a teammate asks how you know the change actually helped. Explain how you'd validate it.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I ran the query again and it felt faster, so I think the clustering key change worked.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: 'Felt faster' is a subjective impression, not evidence, and a single re-run can be misleading on its own — warm cache from the previous run, a quieter warehouse at that moment, or simple variance between runs could all make a query feel faster without the clustering key having mattered at all. This gives no actual numbers, no comparison against a real baseline, and no way to defend the conclusion if someone pushes back on it.
exercises.professionalResponse: Before making the change, I would have captured a baseline using Query Profile and SET STATISTICS-equivalent metrics in Snowflake's own run details — bytes scanned, partitions scanned versus partitions pruned, and total execution time — on a representative, realistic version of the query. After the clustering key change, I'd re-run the same query and compare those same specific numbers directly: did the number of partitions scanned actually drop, which is the real signal that clustering improved pruning, rather than just a faster elapsed time that could be explained by caching or warehouse contention instead. I'd run it more than once to rule out one-off variance, and I'd check whether this was tested on a warehouse in a comparable state both times — ideally freshly resumed, not relying on a result cache from the exact same query run moments earlier, which would make the comparison meaningless. I'd also check Query History over the following days to confirm the improvement holds for the query's normal range of parameter values, not just the one test case I happened to run, since clustering benefits can vary depending on what's actually being filtered for. Only with that direct, repeated, before-and-after comparison — in partitions scanned and execution time, not a subjective impression — would I report this as a proven improvement rather than an assumption.

exercises.title: Validating that an incremental dbt model still produces correct results after a schema change
exercises.situation: A source table gained a new column, and the incremental dbt model built on top of it was updated to include it. A teammate asks how you'd confirm the model is still correct after that change, not just that it builds successfully.
exercises.beginnerResponse: If the dbt run finishes without an error, that means it's working correctly.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: A successful run only proves the SQL is syntactically valid and didn't throw an error — it says nothing about whether the actual data is correct, whether the new column introduced duplicate or missing rows through some interaction with the incremental logic, or whether historical rows that haven't been reprocessed are now inconsistent with newly processed ones. 'It ran' and 'it's correct' are very different claims, and this treats them as the same thing.
exercises.professionalResponse: A successful run only confirms the model compiled and executed without an error — it doesn't confirm the data is correct, so I'd validate that separately and specifically. First, I'd run the project's existing generic tests — not_null, unique, relationships — against the updated model to catch any obvious regressions the schema change might have introduced, like a broken relationship if the new column was meant to support one. Second, since this is an incremental model, I'd specifically check whether the new column is populated correctly for both newly-processed rows and any historical rows, since incremental models by design don't reprocess old data automatically — if the new column needs a value for historical rows too, I'd need a one-time backfill, not just rely on the normal incremental run to fill it in retroactively. Third, I'd run a --full-refresh in a non-production environment and compare its output against the incrementally-built table, row by row on a sample or via an aggregate checksum, to confirm the incremental and full-rebuild paths agree — if the schema change interacts badly with the incremental filter or merge logic in a way that only shows up on a full rebuild, this is exactly how I'd catch it before it surfaces downstream. Finally, I'd add a new test specifically asserting the new column's expected properties going forward, so a future regression here fails the build automatically instead of needing this same manual check repeated by hand.

exercises.title: Deciding between Import and DirectQuery, and proving the choice actually performs
exercises.skillTag: Power BI Import vs. DirectQuery Validation
exercises.situation: A stakeholder wants a Power BI report connected to Snowflake to show data that's always current, with no refresh delay, and asks whether that's possible. Explain the tradeoff and how you'd validate whichever approach you choose.
exercises.beginnerResponse: Sure, I'll just use DirectQuery so it's always live instead of Import, and it should perform fine.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: This agrees to the always-current requirement without naming the real performance cost that comes with it — DirectQuery sends a live query to the source for every interaction, which is often slower than Import's pre-loaded, highly optimized in-memory model — and 'should perform fine' is an assumption, not something that's been checked against this specific report's actual visuals and filters.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd explain the real tradeoff directly: Import loads a copy of the data into Power BI's in-memory model, which is typically much faster to interact with, but it's only as fresh as the last scheduled refresh; DirectQuery sends a live query to Snowflake for every single visual interaction, which gets the freshness they're asking for, but makes report performance directly dependent on Snowflake query speed, every time, for every click. Given that tradeoff, I'd ask how current 'always current' actually needs to be — if a refresh every fifteen minutes would genuinely satisfy the real underlying need, Import with a frequent scheduled refresh often delivers both better performance and 'close enough' freshness, without paying DirectQuery's per-interaction cost. If true real-time is a hard requirement, I'd commit to DirectQuery but validate its actual performance before calling it done, not just assume it: testing the report's real visuals and filters against Snowflake directly, checking whether the warehouse backing it is sized appropriately for this query pattern, and specifically watching for how many separate queries a single dashboard page interaction generates, since DirectQuery reports can silently fire far more queries than expected depending on how visuals interact with each other. I'd also check whether this is a candidate for a hybrid composite model — some tables imported, others live via DirectQuery — if only part of the data genuinely needs to be real-time. Whatever we land on, I'd validate it against the report's actual click-through performance with a representative user, not a one-off test query, before telling the stakeholder it's ready.

exercises.title: Proving a Data Factory Mapping Data Flow tuning change actually improved performance
exercises.skillTag: Data Factory Data Flow Performance Validation
exercises.situation: After adjusting partitioning settings on a slow Mapping Data Flow, a teammate asks how you know the change actually helped, rather than the pipeline just happening to run faster this one time.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I ran the pipeline again and the duration in the monitor was lower, so the change worked.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: A single faster run doesn't rule out normal run-to-run variance — different data volume that day, a less busy integration runtime, or a source system that happened to respond quickly. This never opens Data Flow's own execution details to see where time was actually spent, and never considers testing in debug mode with controlled, comparable conditions before and after the change.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd start by looking at the Data Flow's execution details from the pipeline run, not just the overall duration — it breaks down time spent per transformation stage, which tells me whether the improvement is actually coming from wherever I changed partitioning, or from something else entirely, like the source system simply responding faster that day. Before concluding anything, I'd want a controlled comparison: using Data Flow debug mode with a fixed, representative sample of data, I'd capture stage-level timings before the partitioning change and the same stage-level timings after, holding the data volume and integration runtime conditions as close to identical as I reasonably can. I'd specifically check whether the partition count and distribution actually improved parallelization at the stage I targeted — for instance, whether a transformation that was previously running on too few partitions is now spreading its work more evenly — rather than just noting that the total time went down, which could have other causes. I'd run this comparison more than once, since Data Flow execution can have some run-to-run variance from the underlying Spark-based compute even without any further changes, and I wouldn't trust a single run's improvement as proof. Once that stage-level comparison consistently shows the expected improvement at the specific stage I changed, I'd consider it validated, and I'd note the before-and-after stage timings in whatever documentation accompanies the change, so the next person debugging this pipeline has the actual evidence instead of just a changelog entry saying 'tuned partitioning.'

exercises.title: Proving an Airflow DAG is actually reliable, not just that it hasn't failed recently
exercises.situation: A stakeholder asks whether the nightly orchestrated pipeline is 'reliable' before they start depending on its output for a daily morning report. Explain how you'd actually answer that, beyond 'it's been fine lately.'
exercises.beginnerResponse: It's been running fine for the last couple of weeks, so I'd say yes, it's reliable.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: A short run of recent successes isn't the same as a validated reliability posture — it says nothing about what happens when something does go wrong, whether failures are caught and recovered automatically, how quickly anyone would even find out about a failure, and whether the pipeline would actually make the stakeholder's deadline if a retry were needed. 'It's been fine' is not a property of the system; it's a description of luck so far.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd reframe 'reliable' into specific, checkable properties rather than a track record of luck. First, I'd check whether each task that depends on an external system has an appropriate retry policy with backoff configured, so a transient failure — a brief network blip, a momentary source unavailability — recovers automatically instead of needing a human to notice and intervene. Second, I'd confirm alerting is actually wired up for this DAG specifically, so if a task does fail and exhausts its retries, the team finds out within minutes, not whenever someone happens to check the UI or the stakeholder notices a missing report. Third, I'd look at this DAG's actual historical run durations, including its slower runs, not just its typical ones, and compare that against the time available before the stakeholder's morning deadline — if a retry or two would still comfortably finish before they need the output, that's a real reliability margin; if a single retry would blow past their deadline, 'it's been fine' is masking a real risk that just hasn't materialized yet. Fourth, I'd check whether the tasks involved are idempotent, since that's what makes any retry or manual rerun actually safe rather than risking duplicated data. I'd present reliability as these four specific, verified properties — automatic recovery, prompt alerting, a real time margin against the deadline, and safe retries — rather than a recent streak of successful runs, since that streak doesn't tell the stakeholder what happens the day something actually does go wrong.
